title: Dynamic tenant backpressure and SLA escalation
content:
Purpose and context:

This is a working-note / engineering playbook draft for how the control plane should apply dynamic backpressure, tenant-aware throttles, and escalation paths when per-organization SLAs and noisy-neighbor behavior collide across regions. The goal is pragmatic: keep high-paying customers within contractual latency/availability bounds while protecting overall cluster health and preventing cascading failures across regions.

Scope:
- Routing policy decision surface: per-tenant priority, weight, soft/hard quotas, and regional affinity overrides.
- Control plane responsibilities: decision evaluation, telemetry intake, policy change distribution, and audit logging.
- Runtime mechanisms: request-level throttling, queueing disciplines, circuit breakers, and automated fallbacks (model variant, region, degraded fidelity).
- Escalation & human workflows: auto-notifications, on-call routing changes, and contract-aware compensation steps.

Assumptions and constraints:
- Tenants are classified into four tiers: free, standard, premium, enterprise. Contracts specify latency SLOs (p50/p95) and availability SLAs.
- Serving runtime supports per-tenant token quotas, per-tenant connection limits, streaming vs non-streaming prioritization, and model variant fallbacks.
- Multi-region deployment: us-west, us-east, eu-west, ap-sg (partial). Certain enterprise customers pin to a region for compliance.
- We must avoid hard preemption of enterprise traffic unless a cascade risk is detected. Soft degradation preferred first.

Core concepts and definitions (simple):
- Soft quota: a configurable threshold where request shaping begins (e.g., 70% of committed throughput).
- Hard quota: absolute cap tied to billing or reserved capacity; requests beyond are rejected or routed to lower-cost model.
- Priority weight: numeric weight used in weighted fair scheduling across tenants when overload occurs.
- Fair-share deficit: tenants accumulate deficit to allow small bursts; resets over time window.
- Region affinity: preference to serve a tenant in preferred region; may be overridden for failover.

High-level decision flow (for an incoming request):
1) Authenticate + fetch tenant metadata (tier, reserved capacity, region pins, SLA targets, emergency flags).
2) Evaluate local node/cluster load metrics (queue depth, GPU utilization, estimated tail latency).
3) Check in-flight per-tenant counters (soft quota, hard quota, recent error rate).
4) Compute action using policy engine: allow, shape (delay), batch-queue (lower priority), downgrade (model variant/quantized), reroute (another region/backup pool), reject with SLA-aware code.
5) Emit event to control plane telemetry and attach decision to request trace.

Policy engine details:
- Inputs: tenant tier, token budget, per-route SLO, cluster load, regional capacity, active incidents, tenant blacklists/whitelists.
- Rules are ordered with matching precedence: emergency overrides > contract-honored > fair-share > default.
- Contract-honored rule logic: if tenant has reserved capacity (Dedicated or Private), route to reserved pool; if reserved pool unavailable, attempt enterprise fallback pool before hitting contracted SLA protection.
- Fair-share logic: when cluster load > threshold (eg. 85% util), compute weighted deficit scheduling across active tenants. Each tenant gets min(weighted_share, soft_quota_flush).

Noisy-neighbor mitigation techniques (in order of increasing impact):
1) Adaptive batching knobs: increase batch size for noisy tenant's requests to reduce per-token overhead while capping latency increase.
2) KV/prefix caching: enforce per-tenant cache locality and TTLs; evict aggressively for tenants exceeding cache footprint.
3) Smoothing windows: add short-term smoothing to token emission for tenants with very spiky traffic.
4) Priority demotion: move a tenant from "standard" to a transient lower-priority queue for N minutes while recording metrics and notifying owner.
5) Controlled throttling: insert token-bucket delays at gateway based on soft quota breach.
6) Model downgrades: switch to quantized / smaller model variant (contract-permitted) instead of outright reject.
7) Regional ejection: if tenant is causing local overload and has multi-region tolerance, shift new traffic to another region's pool with capacity.
8) Ejection to cold backup: last resort is to reject or cold-store requests (for batch-only workloads) with clear error codes and SLA escalation.

Backpressure vs. outright rejection policy (recommended):
- Use 3-tier response codes: 200 with "degraded" header (served via lower-fidelity model), 429-throttled (retry-after+reason), 503-reject (when cluster is unsafe to serve).
- Retry semantics must be surfaced to SDKs: recommended exponential backoff, jitter, and an explicit header with suggested fallback model id or region.

SLA-aware behavior matrix (example):
- Enterprise (reserved capacity): honor hard quota; if reserved pool degraded, failover to enterprise-fallback pool with higher-cost compute and notify SRE + account owner. If both fail, trigger executive escalation and potentially issue credits per contract.
- Premium (high-tier non-reserved): protect p95 up to soft quota. During high load, use priority weights to preserve p95 for premium vs standard. If sustained breach > 10min, throttle standard to restore premium SLOs.
- Standard: best-effort; may be demoted or subject to softer downgrades.
- Free: aggressive soft quotas, higher variance allowed; prefer to route to non-critical pools or lower-fidelity models.

Region fallback rules and constraints:
- Respect data residency pins: if tenant requires regional constraint, do not route out-of-region unless explicit emergency flag set on contract.
- Latency tax: when routing cross-region, compute estimated added tail latency and compare against SLA. Only route if acceptable or if tenant-tier permits degraded SLA.
- Warm-pools: maintain small warm pools in secondary regions for enterprise tenants to allow fast failover without cold-start penalties.

Control plane responsibilities and APIs:
- Provide a single policy API: GET /tenant/{id}/routing-decision (returns policy version, weights, quotas, region affinity, active overrides).
- Publish policy change events on a pub/sub channel with versioned diffs; agents subscribe to reconcile locally.
- Audit log all decision overrides for post-mortem and billing adjustments.
- Expose read-only metrics: current weight, soft quota usage, hard quota slack, last decision timestamp.

Telemetry and SLO signals to operate on:
- Per-tenant: request rate, token/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, error rates, model fallback count, throttled count.
- Cluster-level: GPU utilization, queue depth, tail-latency percentiles per node, admission queue sizes.
- Cross-region: inter-region egress latency, failover rate, warm-pool hit rate.
- Alerts: sustained p95 SLA breach per enterprise customer for >5 minutes, noisy tenant causing >X% increase in cluster p99, warm-pool miss >Y times in 15 minutes.

Operational playbook (short):
- Automated first tier: control plane will automatically apply soft-throttles and model downgrades with immediate notification to #infra-alerts.
- SRE escalation: if automatic actions fail to stabilize within 10 minutes, page on-call SRE with runbook pointer and list of affected tenants.
- Account operations: if enterprise contract impacted, auto-generate a support ticket assigned to the customer's CSM and attach audit logs and decision timeline.
- Post-incident: run retrospective with tenant telemetry; propose policy changes and add test cases to chaos harness.

Testing and validation plan:
- Unit tests for policy engine evaluation ordering and precedence.
- Integration tests that simulate multi-tenant spike patterns with synthetic tenants and verify weighted-fair outcomes and fallback behavior.
- Chaos tests: randomly kill warm-pool replicas and ensure failover path respects contract pins and recorded metrics.
- Load tests: validate soft/hard quota thresholds scale linearly and do not introduce systemic tail-latency cliffs.

Rollout plan (phased):
1) Canary on staging: enable policy engine with no-op actions but emit decisions and logs (2 weeks).
2) Canary in prod for low-impact regions: enable shaping but not hard rejections; monitor for 2–3 weeks.
3) Gradual enforcement: enable downgrades and routing fallbacks with 10% traffic sample increase per week.
4) Enterprise opt-in: allow select enterprise customers to test failover and warm-pool routing.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Billing model for use of enterprise-fallback pool during outages (how to surface to finance and customers).
- Exact weight decay function for deficit scheduling — linear vs exponential? (Priya to prototype).
- How to integrate per-route (not just per-tenant) SLAs into the same decision pipeline.
- UX for tenant notification: human-readable reason codes vs numeric codes in SDKs.

References and links (quick):
- Related spec: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PLAT/pages/4567890/Tenant+Routing+Spec
- PR implementing policy engine prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/489
- Jira epic: ENG-2345 (Tenant routing & throttling revamp)

Notes to self:
- Keep this doc intentionally prescriptive but lightweight — the canonical flow should live in the policy engine design doc.
- Add example telemetry dashboards and alert thresholds in next revision.
